historical_sanity_anchors: I-400 design requirement: three Seirans assembled/launched within 30 minutes; Seiran could carry an 800-kg bomb or torpedo.
Historical I-36 conducted an E14Y reconnaissance of Majuro on 22 Apr 1944, demonstrating submarine-air reconnaissance feasibility.
Historical Rainier arrived Majuro 31 May and issued about 1,600 tons of ammunition to TF58 on 1-5 Jun before the 6 Jun sortie.

readiness_and_intelligence.25_29May: I-400/I-401 complete the final joint procedure gate while beginning the long eastbound deployment. Six aircraft become serviceable; minimum five fully mission-ready threshold is passed by 29-30 May.
readiness_and_intelligence.April_recon_retention: The historical I-36 Majuro reconnaissance is retained as an ISR mission even though the low-value Tatsumaki amphibious-tank attack is cancelled; its harbor layout information is stale but useful for planning.
readiness_and_intelligence.30_31May_fresh_packet: Traffic analysis plus a high-speed reconnaissance/submarine observation packet confirms a large carrier/service concentration at Majuro. Exact ship identities are not assumed, but ammunition/oiler/service handling is visibly dense enough to pass the strike-value gate.
readiness_and_intelligence.decision: GO_MAJURO. Do not spend surprise on Eniwetok once the higher-value Majuro packet is confirmed.

mission_design.launch_geometry: I-400 and I-401 approach from a low-traffic sector and launch outside the immediate anchorage ASW ring; simultaneous two-boat deck preparation keeps the total exposure closer to one 30-35 minute cycle per boat rather than serial six-aircraft preparation.
mission_design.load: 800-kg-class bomb centered; support-shipping/ammunition handling is the aim, not carrier search.
mission_design.ingress: pre-dawn low-level/twilight route using known atoll geometry; no broad target search.
mission_design.recovery_policy: Airframes are expendable after attack. Surviving crews are to alight/ditch at a distant prearranged rendezvous for submarine pickup rather than expose the boats to lengthy aircraft crane recovery close to Majuro.

US_damage: USS Rainier (AE-5): one heavy bomb hit/very damaging near-hit sequence centered on cargo-handling/upper works; no magazine catastrophe. Ammunition issue operations stop and the ship becomes locally campaign-out for several days.
One additional fleet-service/oiler target receives moderate splinter/blast damage and leaves the immediate issue line for roughly 2-4 days.
Ammunition handling/lighter/shore-transfer area suffers a secondary fire/explosion; working 180-320 tons of ammunition/special stores destroyed or rendered unusable.
centerline_result.US_air_defense: Radar/visual warning is short. AA and hurried CAP down/disable part of the raid, but the unexpected submarine-aircraft axis prevents a clean interception before all attackers reach weapon range.
centerline_result.I400_I401: Both boats escape the immediate search centerline; no hull loss. Surprise value is consumed and future US anchorage ASW/CAP standards rise sharply.

operational_effect_on_FORAGER.ammunition_issue: Historical 1,600-ton Rainier issue cycle is truncated; branch working issue before/around the strike is roughly 850-1150 tons, with remaining requirements cross-loaded from base/service stocks and other auxiliaries.
operational_effect_on_FORAGER.sortie_effect: FORAGER is NOT cancelled and 15 Jun D-Day is NOT moved. TF58 departure becomes slightly staggered: first elements can sail 6 Jun, while some groups/service-dependent ships lose roughly 8-18 hours to cross-loading/recheck. Reassembly before the 11 Jun strike remains feasible.
operational_effect_on_FORAGER.strategic_value: The raid proves the system and imposes real logistics/security friction, but six aircraft cannot paralyze the US Central Pacific logistics network.

future_effect: US forces now treat submarine-launched aircraft as an operational threat. Majuro/Eniwetok anchorages increase radar/CAP/ASW readiness; future I-400 surprise attacks face materially lower expected value.
